newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil sugar export tax battle comes to a head.
newsitem.headline: Brazil sugar export tax battle comes to a head.

text.p: A battle over how to free up Brazilian sugar exports came to a head Friday when the Central Bank said it cut the export tax to zero the same day the Industry and Commerce Ministry upped export quotas.
"This has really been a battle between two ministries," one trader said.

On Friday, a decree by the Industry and Commerce Ministry increased export quotas by 1.67 million tonnes in the states of Goias, Minas Gerais, Parana, Rio de Janeiro, Santa Catarina and Sao Paulo, the latter getting the lion's share of 1.2 million.
This afternoon however the Central Bank published a circular reducing the tax on all exports of sugar and derivatives to zero which would effectively make the quota increase irrelevant.
Brazilian sugar producers and government officials have been talking for several months over how to free up sugar exports as part of a gradual process to liberalise the entire sector.
Sugar exports traditionally have been governed by quotas set out in the government crop plan issued at the beginning of the season and which are allocated by individual factory.

These quotas can be exported tax-free otherwise they are liable to a 40 percent export tax. Any additional quotas have to be negotiated with the government although in the past this has proved to be a lengthy process.

Producers have been calling for the government to introduce a zero export tax on all exports but have run into resistance from the Industry and Commerce Ministry officials who stressed their preference to increase the export quota allowance to such an extent that it would cover all possible excess sugars.

For producers, the negative aspect of an increase has been the fact the quotas would again be allocated individually and would mean factories with insufficient quota would have to negotiate with those who had quota to spare.

Sugar association officials said they were surprised at both the publication of the additional quotas and the zeroing of the export tax as they said they had understood any decision, although widely anticipated, would be taken next week.
Under the 1997/98 crop plan, Brazil sugar exports were set at 5.39 million tonnes and traders and analysts have said even with a free market, exports are unlikely to exceed 6.5 million.
"This is not going to change much. I think that Brazil's maximum potential is to ship 6.5 million tonnes," said Aloisio Sotero, analyst at independent consultants DataNet-Agricommodities.
What is likely to limit shipments is not such so much sugar availability but logistics such as shipping capacity, he added.
The other key issue is the fact that the export tax is still being retained, albeit at zero.
This still gives the government the power to increase the export quota if it believes that internal sugar and alcohol supply is being compromised.
